findings.title: Blocked-email check is case- and whitespace-sensitive
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the address with an exact BlockedEmail.where(email: email) match, and BlockedEmail only validates uniqueness of the raw email string (no downcasing or stripping in set_defaults). Signup stores whatever the user typed (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] unchanged), while other paths such as change_email normalize with Email.downcase and strip. A blocked row for "bad@spam.com" therefore does not match "Bad@spam.com" or "bad@spam.com ", and the case-sensitive unique index will not treat those as the same address. Someone who was blocked can still register by changing case or surrounding whitespace.

findings.title: Match stats are written inside validation and rolled back or double-counted
findings.body: should_block? is invoked from EmailValidator during User validation, but it is not a pure check: it does match_count += 1, sets last_match_at, and calls save. User#save runs validations inside a transaction and raises ActiveRecord::Rollback when the user is invalid, so the counter update made while rejecting a blocked address is undone and never persisted on a normal save/save!/create. UsersController#create hides this for one path only: it calls user.valid? first (that increment commits) and then user.save (a second increment that rolls back), so the count is right there only by accident and any extra valid? double-counts. The same read-modify-write save also writes every column, so two concurrent matches can lose increments and a concurrent admin change to action_type can be overwritten. Match auditing is unreliable, and the new specs only call should_block? directly so they never catch the rollback.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) after only escaping dots, then uses =~ with no end anchor or domain boundary. A whitelist value of company.com therefore matches user@company.com.attacker.example (and user@company.com.extra) as well as user@company.com, so a site that restricts signup to specific providers can be bypassed by any domain that merely contains the allowed domain as a substring. The same pattern makes a blacklist over-match unrelated hosts such as user@spam.com.legitimate.example. This is now the only server-side domain check (it was moved here from User), and nothing in the new specs covers whitelist or blacklist behavior.
